headline: ダブル is borrowed from English double.
Chikushō is from Middle Chinese 畜生, literally “livestock + livestock; sacrificial animal”, itself influenced by Sanskrit.
コンパス is borrowed from Dutch kompas.
Hagemu is cognate with the adjective 激しい (hageshii), and is possibly はげ (hage) plus む (-mu).
In iyoku, 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾.
コンタクト is from English contact.
レバー is borrowed from English lever.
ドライクリーニング is borrowed from English dry cleaning.
Shinsei is from Middle Chinese 神聖 (MC zyin syengH).
Ya, “arrow”, is from Old Japanese and is found in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Aidagara is 間 (aida, “between; relations”) plus 柄 (-gara, “quality, characteristics”).
Hajiru is from the Old Japanese verb 恥づ.
Tsutsu is from Old Japanese 筒 (tutu), from Proto-Japonic *tutu.
ニュー is borrowed from English new.
Hanabanashii is a reduplication of 花 (hana, “flower”) plus しい (-shii), with hana voiced to bana by rendaku.
Men, “cotton”, is from Middle Chinese 綿 (“wool; cotton; soft, downy”).
Chichi, “milk”, is by surface analysis a reduplication of 乳 (chi).
ソース is from English source.
Yūutsu is from the Middle Chinese compound 憂鬱, literally “worry + melancholy”.
Ho is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *po, and is related to 秀 (ho, “excelling; standing out”).
ブーム is borrowed from English boom.
ファイル is borrowed from English file.
Seijitsu is from Middle Chinese 誠實 (MC dzyeng zyit).
Netsuryō is, by surface analysis, 熱 (netsu) plus 量 (-ryō).
In renmei, 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.
Hirumeshi is 昼 (hiru, “noon”) plus 飯 (meshi, “food; meal”).
Ayamaru is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and may derive from the classical verb ayamu (怪む or 危む).
Shōnika is 小児 (shōni, “infant”) plus 科 (-ka, “course, department”).
Uketsukeru is 受ける (ukeru) plus 付ける (tsukeru).
Ami is a verbal noun of 編む.
クレーン is from English crane, and a doublet of カラン (karan).
